extracted.intended_audience: technology transfer office staff and records managers (university, federal, and similar TT offices)
extracted.subtask_short: records management for technology transfer offices
extracted.subtask_description: Practical records-management techniques and standards tailored to technology transfer (TT) offices for organizing, filing, scanning, labeling, tracking, and processing incoming mail and folders to improve workflow and reduce lost/misfiled documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-quality records management is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality RM is essential to efficient operation of any office; lacking RM leads to missing or empty files and missed deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introduction frames RM as foundational — good RM prevents time-consuming searches, supports informed decisions, and contributes materially to office productivity (examples: NIH-OTT statistics on filings, patents, licenses, royalties). Use this as the guiding principle when evaluating or designing RM systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve organizational systems for incoming mail and folders
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and implement organizational systems specifically for incoming mail and folder populations to streamline routing and reduce misfiling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create clear populations of records and storage locations; ensure incoming-mail handling (sort, date-stamp, file) is standardized (mailroom workflow). Use color-coding, labeling, end-tab design, and database-driven labels to reinforce population separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color-coded multisection folders (folder design and sectioning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use color-coded folders with multiple internal sections so different document categories are separated within a single folder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign distinct colors to different record populations (so misfilings into the wrong population are obvious). Define document categories (recipient/sender/type/chronology/milestone) and create folder sections for each category. Categories should be clearly defined and mutually exclusive so a quick inspection shows where a paper belongs. Provide staff with a miniature booklet or easy reference explaining folder types, colors, and section usage (Table examples given: invention reports, provisional, utility, PCT, foreign, licenses with number of sections and typical contents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use blank off-the-shelf folders with printed adhesive labels rather than custom preprinted folders
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid expensive, fixed preprinted folders; instead use blank folders and print identifying information from the docketing system onto self-adhesive labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printing labels from the database avoids transcription errors, illegible handwriting, and outdated preprinted information. Off-the-shelf folders typically cost less than custom preprinted ones. Use screen prints/labels generated from the docketing system (example: TechTracS) and periodically reprint updated labels to replace outdated ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-piece color-coded end-tab labels for folder identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply one-piece, self-adhesive, custom-designed color-coded labels to folder end-tabs to maximize visual cues for filing and retrieval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design label bands/colors/patterns to create a visual indexing system (e.g., horizontal bands of colors) so misfiled folders stand out. Labels may include numbers, text, logos, color indexes, and bar codes. Use label-printing software (ink-jet/laser) to produce labels. One-piece labels are preferred to rolled/small separate labels because they are more durable and easier to inventory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rolled multi-part labels (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on many small single-character rolled labels for end-tab identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rolled labels (individual character rolls) peel off easily, are damaged more frequently, create inventory problems (running out of common characters), and add time/expense. Prefer one-piece labels printed as needed from software and fed from the docketing system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate filing of incoming mail into folders (mailroom-first filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incoming official mail that belongs in a folder should be filed into that folder in the mailroom before it leaves, rather than handed loose to licensing specialists or others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mailroom should sort, date-stamp, locate the appropriate folder (search CFR if necessary), attach a note to the outside of the folder indicating what was filed, and put the folder into the addressee's inbox. If the folder cannot be located in reasonable time, give a photocopy to the specialist for action while retaining the original until the folder is found. This minimizes loose-paper accumulation and lost documents, and incentivizes returning folders to central filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure incoming correspondence contains critical, easy-to-find information
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure contractor/firm correspondence so key processing and docketing information appears at the beginning in a predictable, numbered list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the categories of information needed (typical law-firm header list suggested): relevant patent application number, country/region, filing date; NIH-OTT docket number; law firm docket number; immediate parent application; inventors; invention title; action requested; preferred response date; statutory/deadline date; work-order number. Encourage contractors to format mail with this numbered list; optionally encode key docketing fields as bar codes to be read directly into the docketing system to eliminate transcription errors. This reduces processing time and clarifies actions and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use docketing system-generated labels and bar codes for consistency and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate front-of-folder labels and bar-coded fields directly from the docketing/database system to avoid handwritten errors and speed indexing/docketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printing labels from the docketing system ensures accurate, legible, and updatable folder identification. Bar-coded docketing information on incoming mail can be read into systems (e.g., with a laser-wand), speeding entry and reducing transcription mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move toward a paperless office by scanning records into the docketing system
rubrics_metrics.description: Scan paper records into electronic form and attach scanned images to the docketing system to provide faster access, improved indexing, and reduced storage costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach scanned images to the relevant record screens in the docketing system so documents and docketed data are linked and accessible to all staff. Scanned images should be indexed according to folder/document categories to speed retrieval. Scanning reduces search/archival labor and can allow destruction of paper archives, but requires planning and quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PDF Image Plus (PDF + OCR) for scanned records
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a scanned-file format that preserves an exact image of the original (PDF) and also applies OCR so text is machine-recognizable and searchable (PDF Image Plus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PDF preserves layout, signatures, date-stamps and handwritten notes; OCR (e.g., ABBYY FineReader) recognizes characters enabling word/phrase searches across documents. PDF Image Plus allows both photographic fidelity and text searchability, enabling faster retrieval and detection of misfiles. PDF alone is simpler but lacks searchable text unless OCR is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan scanning projects carefully (file format, indexing, resolution, workflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do thorough research and planning before undertaking large-scale scanning to choose appropriate hardware/software, file formats, indexing schemes, and resolution, and to avoid logistical pitfalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to address: which hardware/software best fits needs; how scanned images are made available to staff; how images should be indexed; which file format optimizes quality vs size; what scanning resolution balances readability and storage; retention/destruction policy for originals. Engage experienced vendors/consultants for large programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index scanned documents into the same categories used in physical folders
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the same internal category/index scheme used in multisection folders to the electronic index fields so documents can be found quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map folder sections (e.g., correspondence with inventor, documents completed at application filing, law-firm correspondence, references) to electronic index fields/tags in the docketing system so searches and views mirror the physical organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use RFID tags to track folder locations where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Affix passive RFID tags (self-adhesive patches) with a unique identifier to each folder to permit electronic tracking without line-of-sight reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RFID tags contain a microchip and antenna; they can be preprogrammed with random unique IDs (requiring a database mapping) or programmed with human-readable identifiers (docket number). RFID readers with a PDA/transceiver can quickly read multiple folder tags in a location and download data to folder-location tracking software. Consider tag cost (~$1 each) and integration with software (examples: Opus 32). Avoid attaching RFID to metal surfaces; use bar codes for shelf location designations if shelves are metal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folder-location tracking workflow with RFID and PDA/transceiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement a three-step RFID-based location capture: read the shelf/location designation, read RFID tags of folders on that shelf, then download the data into folder-location tracking software to associate folders with locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label each shelf with a unique location-designation (bar code recommended for metal shelving), use a transceiver-PDA to read the shelf code and nearby RFID tags (works at short distance), then upload the pairing to tracking software. This makes it quick to inventory/locate folders and detect misplacements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer RFID over bar codes for bulk folder reading (advantages of RFID)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use RFID instead of bar codes for large inventories because RFID requires no line of sight, reads faster, and reduces re-positioning and read errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bar-code readers need line-of-sight and often fail to read on first try; bar-code labels peel or get damaged. NIH-OTT example: reading ~8,000 folders took 24–32 hours with bar codes versus 4–5 hours with RFID. Use bar codes where RFID is impractical (e.g., metal shelves) or for shelf location labels.
